transcript.content: Hello, welcome to the clinic. Can you tell me what brings you in today?

Hello, Doctor. Yes, well... I've been going back and forth for a little while now about whether I even needed to take up your time, to be completely honest. I'm retired, I have a very quiet life, and I’ve always prided myself on being a very rational, educated person, so I kept telling myself I was just in a bit of a rut and I could think my way out of it. 

But... well, what finally scared me enough to actually pick up the phone and come in today—and I'll admit I almost hung up twice while the receptionist's line was ringing—is that I’ve started having these very unsettling thoughts. It's not like me at all. I’ll just be sitting in my armchair in the evening, maybe reading a book, and this idea will just drift into my head, completely uninvited. I'll catch myself thinking, ‘It would just be simpler if I didn’t wake up tomorrow.’ Just... going to sleep and letting that be the end of it all. 

And I want to be absolutely clear with you right away, because I know how alarming that sounds—I do not have a plan to harm myself. I’m not sitting at home plotting anything terrible or looking through my medicine cabinet. I would never do something like that. But the fact that the thought even occurs to me, that not existing just seems... easier somehow? That really frightened me. I spent all weekend just turning it over and over in my head, wondering how I got to a point where my mind even goes there, and I just realized I couldn't ignore it anymore. It's just a very heavy thing to carry around by yourself.
Have you noticed that you don’t take as much pleasure in things you used to enjoy, or that activities feel more like a chore than they used to?

Yes, actually, that is exactly it. It is so strange you use the word chore, because... well, I’ve been painting with watercolors for, oh, it must be over twenty years now. Ever since I finished my graduate studies and finally had a little time to breathe, it's been my absolute favorite creative outlet. I have this lovely little setup in my sunroom where the morning light is just perfect, and I have a whole ritual for it. I get the jars of water ready, I lay out my good sable brushes, I prep the palette... 

But lately, well, I still set out my watercolor things sometimes, just like I always have. I'll go through the entire physical routine of it, hoping that just the act of preparing will spark something, anything. But then I’ll just sit there at the table, staring at the blank paper. I'll sit there for twenty, thirty minutes sometimes, just looking at it. And then I just... put it all away. I pack it right back into the wooden box without making a single brushstroke, because the pleasure I used to feel in color and light, the way the pigments bleed into the water, it just doesn’t seem to arrive. 

It's completely flat. And it is so terribly frustrating, Doctor, because I have all this free time now in my retirement, time I always promised myself I would spend painting, and instead, the mere thought of actually mixing the paints feels so heavy. I just can't seem to muster the energy to care about the shading or the composition, which is so unlike me, and I just end up washing out the unused water jars feeling entirely empty. It really does feel like a chore, just the expectation that I should be enjoying it makes it feel exhausting.
Have you noticed that your mood has been feeling low or depressed most of the day, nearly every day, rather than just coming and going?

Well, yes. Yes, I suppose that's exactly it. It doesn't really come and go, it's just... there. It’s so strange to try and put into words, because, as I said, I’m a very rational person, and I keep trying to analyze it, to find the root cause, but it’s just this constant, pervasive feeling. 

Most days, it feels as if a gray film has just... settled over everything. And I mean everything. Even in the very small, ordinary moments that used to just be neutral or even a little pleasant. Like when I’m in the kitchen making my morning tea—Earl Grey, usually, with just a splash of milk—or when I’m standing by the window looking out at my garden. I have some lovely hydrangeas out there that I spent years cultivating, and usually, I’d be mentally planning when to prune them or checking the soil dampness. But now, I just look at them and there’s this... this quiet heaviness inside me. 

It’s just a weight, sitting right in my chest, from the moment I wake up until I go to bed. And the most frustrating part is that I can’t quite reason my way out of it. I’ll sit there with my tea, looking at the garden, and I’ll list all the reasons I shouldn't feel this way. I have a comfortable home, my health is generally fine, I have my retirement savings... I’ll go through the whole logical checklist, trying to convince myself that this heaviness is illogical. But the logic doesn't touch it. The gray film just stays there, coloring the whole day, every day. It doesn't lift when the sun comes out or when I try to distract myself with a book. It’s just this constant, quiet companion that I can't seem to shake, no matter how hard I try to think my way around it.
Have you ever experienced a period like this before, where you felt persistently low and lost interest in things you used to enjoy?

No, I really haven't. And that's... well, that's another thing that I've been turning over in my mind endlessly these past few weeks. I mean, I'm sixty-eight years old, Doctor. I've lived a full life, I've been through my share of ups and downs, as anyone my age has. When my husband passed away, oh, it must be twelve years ago now... well, naturally, I grieved. It was a terrible, sharp sort of pain, and there were days I didn't want to get out of bed, but it felt different. It felt like a reaction to something real, something tangible. I knew exactly why I was sad, and even in the midst of it, I still found comfort in reading, or listening to classical music—Bach, mostly, I've always found his counterpoint very soothing when my mind is unsettled. 

But this? This current state of affairs? It's entirely unprecedented for me. I've always been the sort of person who just... carried on. When I was working on my dissertation, pulling those dreadful all-nighters, or when I was managing the archives at the university, dealing with all the departmental politics—which, let me tell you, could be quite exhausting—I always had this core of resilience. I could always find a reason to be engaged with the world, even if I was tired or stressed. I always had my painting, or my garden, or my reading group. 

So to answer your question, no, I have never experienced this kind of persistent, unshakeable emptiness before. Not like this, where there's no obvious trigger, no external event to point to and say, 'Ah, yes, that is why the world has gone gray.' It’s completely foreign to me, which I suppose is why I spent so much time trying to intellectualize it away before finally admitting defeat and coming to see you. It just doesn't fit with my understanding of myself, or how my mind has operated for the last six decades.
Have you ever had a period in the past when you felt down or lost interest in things for more than two weeks at a time?

Well, as I was just saying, no, not really. I mean, certainly not for two weeks at a time, and certainly not like this. I was just thinking about this the other day, actually, when I was sitting in the sunroom, looking at my watercolor brushes and feeling that awful, heavy blankness I mentioned earlier. I started trying to mentally catalog every difficult period in my life, going all the way back to my twenties. 

I thought about the time right after I finished my master's degree—I was twenty-four, I think, or maybe twenty-five—and I was so terribly burnt out. I spent a week just sleeping and reading mystery novels, barely leaving my apartment. But that was just exhaustion, you see? I was tired, yes, but I still enjoyed the novels. I still enjoyed a good cup of coffee in the morning. And it only lasted a few days before I was itching to get back to the library and start my doctoral research. 

And then, of course, there was the period after my husband passed. That was a profound sadness, a real, visceral grief. There were weeks, maybe even a month or two, where everything felt incredibly difficult. The house felt too quiet, the evenings were too long... but even then, Doctor, even in the absolute thick of it, it wasn't this... this utter lack of interest. I still cared about things, even if they made me sad. I still wanted to tend to the garden, because he had loved the hydrangeas so much. I still listened to my Bach recordings, even if I cried while doing it. 

But this current situation, where the world just feels entirely flat and colorless for weeks on end? Where I don't even have the energy to care that I don't care? No, I've never had a stretch like this before. Not for two weeks, not for two months. It's completely novel, and as I said, it's just so terribly frustrating because it defies all my attempts to logically dismantle it. I just keep trying to find a precedent for it in my own history, a time where I felt this specific brand of emptiness, so I could say, 'Ah, yes, I survived this in 1985, I can survive it now.' But there simply isn't one. It's uncharted territory for me, which is quite a disconcerting feeling at sixty-eight, I must admit.

Have you ever had a period in your life, even before retirement or before the loss of your husband, where you felt down or uninterested in things for a few weeks or more, even if you didn’t talk about it or seek help for it at the time?

I can see why you’re pressing the point, Doctor, I really can. You’re being thorough, and perhaps you’re wondering if I was the sort of person who just suffered in silence, keeping up appearances. Heaven knows my generation was practically raised on the concept of the stiff upper lip, and especially in academia... well. When I was starting out in the department in the late seventies, showing any sort of emotional vulnerability was practically professional suicide for a woman. So, it's a very logical question for you to ask—did I just hide it? Did I just put on a brave face and push through?

But the honest answer is still no. Even in my absolute most private moments, even when the door was shut and I was entirely alone with my own thoughts... I never felt this way. I've always been fiercely introspective, almost to a fault, as you can probably tell by now. I keep a journal—have done since I was a teenager, actually, volumes and volumes of them sitting on the bottom shelves of my bookcase—and if I had ever gone through a spell of this... this terrible, flat apathy for weeks on end, I would have analyzed it to death on the page. 

I mean, there were incredibly stressful times that I didn't broadcast to the world, certainly. I remember in, oh, it must have been 1988, when the university slashed our departmental budget and I had to fight tooth and nail just to keep the archives functioning properly. I was furious, I was stressed, I lost sleep, and I certainly didn't go to a therapist about it. But I wasn't *empty*. I was full of fire, actually! I was drafting memos at two in the morning, pacing the floorboards. I was deeply, intensely engaged with the problem. 

That’s the difference, you see? Even when things were difficult, or when I kept my personal struggles entirely to myself, I always had my drive. I never had this feeling of the color being drained out of the world, where I just didn't care. So no, not even in secret, not even in my younger years. This is entirely, bafflingly new, which is why I'm having such a dreadful time trying to make sense of it.
Have you ever had a period in your life before this one where you felt persistently down or uninterested in things for at least two weeks, even if you didn’t talk about it or seek help at the time?

I... well, Doctor, I feel as though we might be going around in circles just a bit here. I do understand why you keep asking, I really do. In my own research—historical archives, as I mentioned—we always looked for precedents. It’s human nature to want to find a pattern, to establish a timeline. But I must tell you, definitively and absolutely, no. Not for two weeks, not for ten days... never. 

I've combed through my memories since we started talking, trying to find some hidden moment for you. I even just now thought about when my daughter went off to university—empty nest syndrome, they call it. I missed her terribly, of course. The house was so dreadfully quiet without her practicing the piano every afternoon. But did I lose interest in my life? Did I feel this awful, persistent flatness? Absolutely not. I immediately threw myself into a massive new cataloging project at the library. I was energized, if anything, by the extra time I had to dedicate to my work and my garden. 

So, no matter how many different ways we look at it or phrase it, the answer is just... no. I have never, in my sixty-eight years on this earth, experienced a two-week period of this grayness. My mind has always been active, always engaged, always caring deeply about *something*, even if it was just a good book or a difficult piece of music. It’s completely unprecedented. And quite frankly, it’s a bit exhausting trying to conjure up a ghost in my past that simply isn't there. I've always been a person who feels things very vividly, whether it's joy or sorrow, and this current... nothingness... is just entirely alien to my nature.
Have you ever had a time before this one where you felt persistently down or lost interest in most things for at least two weeks in a row?

Doctor, I... I must confess I am entirely baffled now. We seem to be completely stuck on this one specific point, and I truly do not know how else to express to you that the answer is no. I feel a bit like I'm taking an oral examination for my doctorate all over again and repeatedly giving the wrong answer to the committee! But I can only give you the truth, and the truth hasn't changed since the last three times we went over it. 

I have sat here and practically given you my entire autobiography—from my twenties, to my husband's passing, to my daughter leaving for school. I’m starting to wonder if perhaps you think I’m forgetting something? At sixty-eight, I suppose it's entirely fair for a doctor to question a patient's memory, but my mind is quite sharp, I assure you. 

While you were just asking me that again, I was even trying to think if perhaps a physical illness ever laid me low for two weeks and made me feel this way, just to give you *something* to work with. I had a dreadful bout of pneumonia in the winter of '94, I believe it was. I was bedridden for nearly a month. I felt terrible, physically speaking, weak as a kitten, coughing constantly. But mentally? I was so incredibly bored and frustrated that I couldn't get up and go to the archives! I was practically begging my neighbor, Susan, to bring me crossword puzzles and library books. I didn't lose interest in things, I just lacked the physical lung capacity to do them. 

So, please, you simply must believe me when I say this. No. Never before this current situation have I ever felt down or uninterested in my life for two weeks in a row. Not ever. I truly hope we can move on to whatever the next question is, because I'm quite out of historical examples to prove my point to you.
Have you ever experienced a period of time when your mood was unusually elevated, irritable, or you felt extremely energetic for several days or more?

Oh, thank heavens, a new question! I was genuinely starting to worry we were going to be trapped in that previous topic for the rest of the afternoon. 

But to answer this new one... unusually elevated or extremely energetic. Well, I suppose it really depends on what you consider 'extreme,' doesn't it? As I mentioned just a moment ago with the budget crisis in '88, or when I was deep into a massive cataloging project, I could certainly be very focused and driven. I could stay up late working, entirely engrossed in the minutiae of it all. But that was just dedication to my field. It wasn't an unusual elevation of my mood. It was entirely proportional to whatever project or crisis I was tackling at the time. I've never had a period where I was just inexplicably buzzing with energy for days on end, or feeling somehow euphoric or out of control for no earthly reason. 

I've always been a very grounded, methodical sort of person. You simply don't spend forty years organizing and preserving historical documents if you're prone to wild flights of fancy or erratic bursts of energy. It requires a very steady hand and a very steady mind. 

And as for being irritable for days at a time... well, I can be quite particular, I'll admit that. If an undergraduate mishandled a delicate nineteenth-century manuscript, I would certainly give them a very sharp piece of my mind! Or if my late husband left his muddy gardening boots right on the entryway rug after I'd just swept... yes, I’d be annoyed. But that’s just a normal, fleeting reaction to a specific annoyance, isn't it? It certainly never stretched into a persistent, irritable mood that lasted for days. 

My temperament has just always been very even-keeled. My husband actually used to tease me that I was the most predictably level-headed woman in the county. It's just not in my constitution to swing wildly in that direction. So no, I haven't experienced anything like what you're describing there, either.
Can you tell me when these feelings of persistent low mood and loss of interest in your usual activities first started?

Well, let me think back... it's been quite a stretch now. I'd say it's been going on for about eight months. Yes, eight months almost exactly. It all started around the time my brother's health took that terrible turn, and his behavior changed so suddenly. 

He's always been such a robust man, you see—always out fixing things, tinkering with old cars, never one to sit still. And then, almost overnight, it was like a switch flipped. He became so frail, and his mind... well, it just wasn't the same. He started getting confused, agitated, forgetting things we'd talked about just hours before. It was profoundly unsettling to witness. I've always been the organized one in the family, the one who handles the paperwork and the planning, so naturally, a lot of the responsibility for sorting out his care fell to me. 

And I think that's when this... this grayness really began to settle over me. I was spending hours on the phone with doctors, insurance companies, trying to arrange home aides—which is a nightmare in and of itself, let me tell you, the sheer amount of bureaucracy involved is staggering. And amidst all that chaos, I just realized one day that I hadn't touched my cataloging project in weeks. I hadn't been out to the garden, even though it was the perfect time for planting bulbs. The thought of doing those things, things I've loved for decades, just felt entirely pointless. It was like all the color had just drained out of my world right alongside his health. So yes, eight months of this... this absolute flatness.

Have you had any distinct period or episode when you felt down nearly every day, lost interest in things, or had other symptoms of depression that lasted for at least two weeks but less than two years?

Doctor, I... well, I must admit I am completely flabbergasted now. Are we truly circling back to this again? I feel as though we are trapped in some sort of conversational loop! As I stated quite explicitly just a little while ago, before these past eight months with my brother’s decline, I have never, ever experienced a period like this. Not for two weeks, not for two months, and certainly not for anything approaching two years. 

I mean, logically speaking, if I haven't had a two-week period of this... this awful grayness in my entire life prior to now, then I couldn't possibly have had one lasting up to two years, could I? It’s just basic deduction. I’ve kept a daily planner and a personal journal since I was in graduate school—since the autumn of 1979, to be exact. I have boxes of them meticulously labeled in my study. If I had lost interest in my life for weeks or months on end at any point in my thirties, forties, or fifties, there would be a glaring, undeniable gap in the archival record of my own life! But there isn't. 

Even when my husband passed, which was a profound and terrible grief, of course, I didn't lose interest in the world. I threw myself into organizing his estate, I kept up with my library board meetings, I made sure my daughter was supported. I grieved, yes, but I wasn't... empty, the way I am now. I didn't lose my drive. 

So, no. No to two weeks, no to two years, no to any timeframe you might suggest prior to eight months ago. It is just these past eight months, since my brother got sick. I really do hope we can move forward to the next topic now, Doctor, because I am quite literally running out of ways to say 'never before.'
Have you ever had a time when you felt down or lost interest in things for more than two years at a time, but not continuously until now?

Doctor, I... I must confess I am entirely at a loss here. I am sitting here, looking at you, and I am genuinely wondering if we are speaking the same language, or if perhaps I am not articulating myself with the clarity I have always prided myself on. 

We just established—not five minutes ago, and indeed, not one minute ago—that prior to these last eight months, I have never experienced this sort of profound emptiness. Not for two weeks. Not for two months. And so, it follows, as surely as night follows day, that I could not possibly have experienced it for more than two years! 

It's... it's a matter of simple chronological logic, isn't it? If the total sum of my experience with this... this dreadful, gray state of being is exactly eight months, beginning precisely when my brother's health collapsed, then how on earth could there be a two-year period lurking somewhere in my past? There simply isn't room for it in the timeline of my life! 

I feel as though I am testifying before a particularly stubborn committee, repeating the same basic facts into the record over and over again. As I told you, I have lived a very engaged, very active life. I spent thirty-five years at the university library, managing special collections. You do not maintain that level of employment, let alone the meticulousness required for archival work, if you are spending years—years!—losing interest in the world around you. 

Even during the difficult periods—and goodness knows, everyone has them, like the budget cuts in the early nineties that nearly decimated our acquisitions department, or, as I mentioned, the passing of my dear husband—I was always present. I was always functioning, always interested in my work, my family, my garden. The idea that I could have spent more than two years feeling the way I do now, and somehow forgotten it, or failed to document it in my journals... well, it's just preposterous. 

So, for what I sincerely hope is the very last time on this particular nuance of the timeline: no. No, I have never felt this way for more than two years. It is just these past eight months. That is the entirety of it. Can we please, I beg of you, move on to whatever is next on your clipboard?

I’ll go through the whole logical checklist, trying to convince myself that this heaviness is illogical. But the logic doesn't touch it. The gray film just stays there, coloring the whole day, every day. It doesn't lift when the sun comes out or when I try to distract myself with a book. It’s just this constant, quiet companion that I can't seem to shake, no matter how hard I try to think my way around it.

No, I really haven't. And that's... well, that's another thing that I've been turning over in my mind endlessly these past few weeks. I mean, I'm sixty-eight years old, Doctor. I've lived a full life, I've been through my share of ups and downs, as anyone my age has. When my husband passed away, oh, it must be twelve years ago now... well, naturally, I grieved. It was a terrible, sharp sort of pain, and there were days I didn't want to get out of bed, but it felt different. It felt like a reaction to something real, something tangible. I knew exactly why I was sad, and even in the midst of it, I still found comfort in reading, or listening to classical music—Bach, mostly, I've always found his counterpoint very soothing when my mind is unsettled. 

But this? This current state of affairs? It's entirely unprecedented for me. I've always been the sort of person who just... carried on. When I was working on my dissertation, pulling those dreadful all-nighters, or when I was managing the archives at the university, dealing with all the departmental politics—which, let me tell you, could be quite exhausting—I always had this core of resilience. I could always find a reason to be engaged with the world, even if I was tired or stressed. I always had my painting, or my garden, or my reading group. 

So to answer your question, no, I have never experienced this kind of persistent, unshakeable emptiness before. Not like this, where there's no obvious trigger, no external event to point to and say, 'Ah, yes, that is why the world has gone gray.' It’s completely foreign to me, which I suppose is why I spent so much time trying to intellectualize it away before finally admitting defeat and coming to see you. It just doesn't fit with my understanding of myself, or how my mind has operated for the last six decades.

patient.answer:
Well, as I was just saying, no, not really. I mean, certainly not for two weeks at a time, and certainly not like this. I was just thinking about this the other day, actually, when I was sitting in the sunroom, looking at my watercolor brushes and feeling that awful, heavy blankness I mentioned earlier. I started trying to mentally catalog every difficult period in my life, going all the way back to my twenties. 

I thought about the time right after I finished my master's degree—I was twenty-four, I think, or maybe twenty-five—and I was so terribly burnt out. I spent a week just sleeping and reading mystery novels, barely leaving my apartment. But that was just exhaustion, you see? I was tired, yes, but I still enjoyed the novels. I still enjoyed a good cup of coffee in the morning. And it only lasted a few days before I was itching to get back to the library and start my doctoral research. 

And then, of course, there was the period after my husband passed. That was a profound sadness, a real, visceral grief. There were weeks, maybe even a month or two, where everything felt incredibly difficult. The house felt too quiet, the evenings were too long... but even then, Doctor, even in the absolute thick of it, it wasn't this... this utter lack of interest. I still cared about things, even if they made me sad. I still wanted to tend to the garden, because he had loved the hydrangeas so much. I still listened to my Bach recordings, even if I cried while doing it. 

But this current situation, where the world just feels entirely flat and colorless for weeks on end? Where I don't even have the energy to care that I don't care? No, I've never had a stretch like this before. Not for two weeks, not for two months. It's completely novel, and as I said, it's just so terribly frustrating because it defies all my attempts to logically dismantle it. I just keep trying to find a precedent for it in my own history, a time where I felt this specific brand of emptiness, so I could say, 'Ah, yes, I survived this in 1985, I can survive it now.' But there simply isn't one. It's uncharted territory for me, which is quite a disconcerting feeling at sixty-eight, I must admit.

patient.answer:
I can see why you’re pressing the point, Doctor, I really can. You’re being thorough, and perhaps you’re wondering if I was the sort of person who just suffered in silence, keeping up appearances. Heaven knows my generation was practically raised on the concept of the stiff upper lip, and especially in academia... well. When I was starting out in the department in the late seventies, showing any sort of emotional vulnerability was practically professional suicide for a woman. So, it's a very logical question for you to ask—did I just hide it? Did I just put on a brave face and push through?

But the honest answer is still no. Even in my absolute most private moments, even when the door was shut and I was entirely alone with my own thoughts... I never felt this way. I've always been fiercely introspective, almost to a fault, as you can probably tell by now. I keep a journal—have done since I was a teenager, actually, volumes and volumes of them sitting on the bottom shelves of my bookcase—and if I had ever gone through a spell of this... this terrible, flat apathy for weeks on end, I would have analyzed it to death on the page. 

I mean, there were incredibly stressful times that I didn't broadcast to the world, certainly. I remember in, oh, it must have been 1988, when the university slashed our departmental budget and I had to fight tooth and nail just to keep the archives functioning properly. I was furious, I was stressed, I lost sleep, and I certainly didn't go to a therapist about it. But I wasn't *empty*. I was full of fire, actually! I was drafting memos at two in the morning, pacing the floorboards. I was deeply, intensely engaged with the problem. 

That’s the difference, you see? Even when things were difficult, or when I kept my personal struggles entirely to myself, I always had my drive. I never had this feeling of the color being drained out of the world, where I just didn't care. So no, not even in secret, not even in my younger years. This is entirely, bafflingly new, which is why I'm having such a dreadful time trying to make sense of it.

patient.answer:
I... well, Doctor, I feel as though we might be going around in circles just a bit here. I do understand why you keep asking, I really do. In my own research—historical archives, as I mentioned—we always looked for precedents. It’s human nature to want to find a pattern, to establish a timeline. But I must tell you, definitively and absolutely, no. Not for two weeks, not for ten days... never. 

I've combed through my memories since we started talking, trying to find some hidden moment for you. I even just now thought about when my daughter went off to university—empty nest syndrome, they call it. I missed her terribly, of course. The house was so dreadfully quiet without her practicing the piano every afternoon. But did I lose interest in my life? Did I feel this awful, persistent flatness? Absolutely not. I immediately threw myself into a massive new cataloging project at the library. I was energized, if anything, by the extra time I had to dedicate to my work and my garden. 

So, no matter how many different ways we look at it or phrase it, the answer is just... no. I have never, in my sixty-eight years on this earth, experienced a two-week period of this grayness. My mind has always been active, always engaged, always caring deeply about *something*, even if it was just a good book or a difficult piece of music. It’s completely unprecedented. And quite frankly, it’s a bit exhausting trying to conjure up a ghost in my past that simply isn't there. I've always been a person who feels things very vividly, whether it's joy or sorrow, and this current... nothingness... is just entirely alien to my nature.

patient.answer:
Doctor, I... I must confess I am entirely baffled now. We seem to be completely stuck on this one specific point, and I truly do not know how else to express to you that the answer is no. I feel a bit like I'm taking an oral examination for my doctorate all over again and repeatedly giving the wrong answer to the committee! But I can only give you the truth, and the truth hasn't changed since the last three times we went over it. 

I have sat here and practically given you my entire autobiography—from my twenties, to my husband's passing, to my daughter leaving for school. I’m starting to wonder if perhaps you think I’m forgetting something? At sixty-eight, I suppose it's entirely fair for a doctor to question a patient's memory, but my mind is quite sharp, I assure you. 

While you were just asking me that again, I was even trying to think if perhaps a physical illness ever laid me low for two weeks and made me feel this way, just to give you *something* to work with. I had a dreadful bout of pneumonia in the winter of '94, I believe it was. I was bedridden for nearly a month. I felt terrible, physically speaking, weak as a kitten, coughing constantly. But mentally? I was so incredibly bored and frustrated that I couldn't get up and go to the archives! I was practically begging my neighbor, Susan, to bring me crossword puzzles and library books. I didn't lose interest in things, I just lacked the physical lung capacity to do them. 

So, please, you simply must believe me when I say this. No. Never before this current situation have I ever felt down or uninterested in my life for two weeks in a row. Not ever. I truly hope we can move on to whatever the next question is, because I'm quite out of historical examples to prove my point to you.

patient.answer:
Oh, thank heavens, a new question! I was genuinely starting to worry we were going to be trapped in that previous topic for the rest of the afternoon. 

But to answer this new one... unusually elevated or extremely energetic. Well, I suppose it really depends on what you consider 'extreme,' doesn't it? As I mentioned just a moment ago with the budget crisis in '88, or when I was deep into a massive cataloging project, I could certainly be very focused and driven. I could stay up late working, entirely engrossed in the minutiae of it all. But that was just dedication to my field. It wasn't an unusual elevation of my mood. It was entirely proportional to whatever project or crisis I was tackling at the time. I've never had a period where I was just inexplicably buzzing with energy for days on end, or feeling somehow euphoric or out of control for no earthly reason. 

I've always been a very grounded, methodical sort of person. You simply don't spend forty years organizing and preserving historical documents if you're prone to wild flights of fancy or erratic bursts of energy. It requires a very steady hand and a very steady mind. 

And as for being irritable for days at a time... well, I can be quite particular, I'll admit that. If an undergraduate mishandled a delicate nineteenth-century manuscript, I would certainly give them a very sharp piece of my mind! Or if my late husband left his muddy gardening boots right on the entryway rug after I'd just swept... yes, I’d be annoyed. But that’s just a normal, fleeting reaction to a specific annoyance, isn't it? It certainly never stretched into a persistent, irritable mood that lasted for days. 

My temperament has just always been very even-keeled. My husband actually used to tease me that I was the most predictably level-headed woman in the county. It's just not in my constitution to swing wildly in that direction. So no, I haven't experienced anything like what you're describing there, either.

patient.answer:
Well, let me think back... it's been quite a stretch now. I'd say it's been going on for about eight months. Yes, eight months almost exactly. It all started around the time my brother's health took that terrible turn, and his behavior changed so suddenly. 

He's always been such a robust man, you see—always out fixing things, tinkering with old cars, never one to sit still. And then, almost overnight, it was like a switch flipped. He became so frail, and his mind... well, it just wasn't the same. He started getting confused, agitated, forgetting things we'd talked about just hours before. It was profoundly unsettling to witness. I've always been the organized one in the family, the one who handles the paperwork and the planning, so naturally, a lot of the responsibility for sorting out his care fell to me. 

And I think that's when this... this grayness really began to settle over me. I was spending hours on the phone with doctors, insurance companies, trying to arrange home aides—which is a nightmare in and of itself, let me tell you, the sheer amount of bureaucracy involved is staggering. And amidst all that chaos, I just realized one day that I hadn't touched my cataloging project in weeks. I hadn't been out to the garden, even though it was the perfect time for planting bulbs. The thought of doing those things, things I've loved for decades, just felt entirely pointless. It was like all the color had just drained out of my world right alongside his health. So yes, eight months of this... this absolute flatness.

As I stated quite explicitly just a little while ago, before these past eight months with my brother’s decline, I have never, ever experienced a period like this. Not for two weeks, not for two months, and certainly not for anything approaching two years. 

I mean, logically speaking, if I haven't had a two-week period of this... this awful grayness in my entire life prior to now, then I couldn't possibly have had one lasting up to two years, could I? It’s just basic deduction. I’ve kept a daily planner and a personal journal since I was in graduate school—since the autumn of 1979, to be exact. I have boxes of them meticulously labeled in my study. If I had lost interest in my life for weeks or months on end at any point in my thirties, forties, or fifties, there would be a glaring, undeniable gap in the archival record of my own life! But there isn't. 

Even when my husband passed, which was a profound and terrible grief, of course, I didn't lose interest in the world. I threw myself into organizing his estate, I kept up with my library board meetings, I made sure my daughter was supported. I grieved, yes, but I wasn't... empty, the way I am now. I didn't lose my drive. 

So, no. No to two weeks, no to two years, no to any timeframe you might suggest prior to eight months ago. It is just these past eight months, since my brother got sick. I really do hope we can move forward to the next topic now, Doctor, because I am quite literally running out of ways to say 'never before.'

patient.answer:
Doctor, I... I must confess I am entirely at a loss here. I am sitting here, looking at you, and I am genuinely wondering if we are speaking the same language, or if perhaps I am not articulating myself with the clarity I have always prided myself on. 

We just established—not five minutes ago, and indeed, not one minute ago—that prior to these last eight months, I have never experienced this sort of profound emptiness. Not for two weeks. Not for two months. And so, it follows, as surely as night follows day, that I could not possibly have experienced it for more than two years! 

It's... it's a matter of simple chronological logic, isn't it? If the total sum of my experience with this... this dreadful, gray state of being is exactly eight months, beginning precisely when my brother's health collapsed, then how on earth could there be a two-year period lurking somewhere in my past? There simply isn't room for it in the timeline of my life! 

I feel as though I am testifying before a particularly stubborn committee, repeating the same basic facts into the record over and over again. As I told you, I have lived a very engaged, very active life. I spent thirty-five years at the university library, managing special collections. You do not maintain that level of employment, let alone the meticulousness required for archival work, if you are spending years—years!—losing interest in the world around you. 

Even during the difficult periods—and goodness knows, everyone has them, like the budget cuts in the early nineties that nearly decimated our acquisitions department, or, as I mentioned, the passing of my dear husband—I was always present. I was always functioning, always interested in my work, my family, my garden. The idea that I could have spent more than two years feeling the way I do now, and somehow forgotten it, or failed to document it in my journals... well, it's just preposterous. 

So, for what I sincerely hope is the very last time on this particular nuance of the timeline: no. No, I have never felt this way for more than two years. It is just these past eight months. That is the entirety of it. Can we please, I beg of you, move on to whatever is next on your clipboard?
